answers.answer: One row per SNP with its location, alleles, effect size, standard error and P-value
answers.feedback: Right. Summary statistics summarize every variant-trait association tested in the GWAS.

answers.answer: The genotypes of every person in the GWAS
answers.feedback: Those are individual-level data. Summary statistics contain no information about individual people, which is why they can be shared publicly.

answers.answer: Only the SNPs that pass P < 5 × 10⁻⁸
answers.feedback: Full summary statistics include every SNP tested, not just the genome-wide significant ones. A PRS often uses many SNPs below the threshold.

answers.answer: A list of the genes near each GWAS peak
answers.feedback: Mapped genes are sometimes added, but summary statistics are the per-SNP statistical results.

question: Which of these is a GWAS analysis result (a statistical coefficient) rather than variant location information?

answers.feedback: Right. Effect size, standard error and P-value come from the association test; chromosome, position, rsID and alleles locate and describe the variant.
The rsID is an identifier for the variant, part of its location information.
Chromosome and position say where the variant is.
The alleles describe the variant itself; the effect size is the result of the test.

question: Why can a polygenic risk score be built without access to the individual-level data from the original GWAS?

answers.answer: The summary statistics give the variants, effect alleles and weights the score needs
answers.feedback: Right. A PRS needs to know which allele to count at each SNP and how much weight to give it, and both are in the summary statistics.

answers.answer: A PRS only uses the single most significant SNP
answers.feedback: A PRS combines many SNPs — that is what 'polygenic' means.

answers.answer: The people being scored must also have been in the GWAS
answers.feedback: The opposite: the people being scored (target data) should not overlap with the GWAS (base data). See the quality-control module.

question: Each tower of points above the 5 × 10⁻⁸ line in a Manhattan plot is best described as…

answers.answer: A locus: many correlated SNPs carrying the same association signal
answers.feedback: Right. SNPs in linkage disequilibrium with a causal variant rise together, so each peak is a locus rather than a single SNP.
Most points in a tower are SNPs in LD with the causal variant, which is usually not known. This matters for PRS (clumping, in the second lecture).

answers.answer: A gene that causes the disease
answers.feedback: GWAS locate associated regions; which gene (if any) is responsible needs further work.
